A specific texture associated with the event

Maladaptive Strategies.value: give up important responsibilities to stay safe or avoid triggers
I drift off into a world of my own
make sure never to be alone with another person

Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
I feel like an object, not like a person
You can never know who will harm you

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

issues.item: Threat: missing/none selected despite multiple current-danger and exposure-related items
issues.explanation: The profile contains several items implying an active sense of present threat or exposure (e.g., 'World is Dangerous', 'Exposed to Others', concealment to avoid being noticed), yet the Threat component is entirely absent. For this trauma type, such items would usually cohere with at least some explicit threat content; the omission makes the cross-node picture clinically uneven.

'World is Dangerous' expresses a broad ongoing threat belief, but the formulation specifies no active links into or out of Threat and no Threat items are endorsed. This makes the appraisal sit awkwardly in the formulation because it functions more like a threat belief than an isolated negative self-appraisal.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed
issues.explanation: 'Concealing Clothing ... to avoid being noticed' implies active management of current interpersonal threat/visibility. With Threat completely unrepresented and no Trigger→Threat or Maladaptive Strategies→Threat linkage in the formulation, this strategy lacks a clear matching symptom target in the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
issues.explanation: The Threat node is not clinically coherent here. 'Flashbacks' and 'Physical Reactivity' are re-experiencing/arousal responses rather than threat appraisals, while the only genuine threat appraisal selected is 'Threat from Strangers.' That mixes different constructs within one node.

vignette: Marcus Vance was ten years old the first time his stepfather’s hands closed around his wrists in the basement. The abuse never followed a predictable schedule, which meant Marcus learned to measure danger in shifts of light and sound. It almost always came at night, when the basement windows were black and the house settled into silence. His stepfather would drag him toward the corner where a heavy, scratchy wool blanket was stored, a texture that would bite his ankles and forearms as it was pulled over him. Sometimes, from upstairs, the muffled whimpers of his younger half-brother would filter through the floorboards, a sound that seemed to amplify the terror rather than distract from it. Marcus did not understand then why he could not simply run; he only knew that when the darkness pooled in the corners and that rough wool touched his skin, his body locked into a frantic stillness. Over the years, those nights followed him into his waking hours. By the time Marcus was fifteen, the basement’s shadowed corners had become a recurring film in his mind, looping every time he closed his eyes. The memories arrived with the weight of his stepfather’s grip, the bite of the wool, the cold air, and the echoing cries. When the sensation hit, the emotion became so dense he had to physically step away from whatever he was doing, his breath catching until the wave passed. He began to notice that people seemed to see right through him, as if the history of his body were printed on his skin. He felt less like a person and more like something handled, measured, and discarded. Along with that sense of exposure, he carried a steady certainty that harm could arrive from any direction, at any moment, from anyone he thought he knew. Now twenty-five and working as a housekeeper, Marcus’s daily route takes him through apartments where he hangs linens, strips mattresses, and vacuums hallways. The work should be straightforward, but the tactile demands have become a constant minefield. Two weeks ago, while stripping a king-sized bed in a client’s guest room, his fingers brushed against a thick, nubby wool throw left folded on the chair. The moment the fabric caught his skin, the memory replayed in full sensory reliving; the basement air returned, his wrists burned, and the sound of a child crying seemed to emanate from the ventilation grate. He dropped the sheet, his heart hammering against his ribs, and had to step out into the hallway until the physical trembling subsided. He told his supervisor he felt unwell and took the rest of the day off, a pattern that has cost him three overtime shifts this month. He has come to believe that dropping responsibilities keeps him safe. He quietly turns down assignments that require solo work in dimly lit storage rooms or late-night callouts. Marcus has also stopped answering calls after eight o’clock. He cannot bear the quiet that follows, nor the way the dark seems to press against his windows. When he needs to sleep, he keeps his bedroom door wide open and leaves a hallway light on, but he still sleeps with one eye peeled to the ceiling. He refuses to spend evenings alone in his own apartment, instead lingering in the lobby of the grocery store or sitting in the corner of a brightly lit diner until someone else walks in. He tells himself it is just caution, that it is wise to know who is in the room, but what frightens him most is the steady expectation that the floor could give way without warning. He tried to escape the rising panic by letting his mind drift into elaborate mental landscapes. The drift became a refuge he leaned into whenever work grew too loud or too close. He realized he was losing track of his own schedule, his own name, and his own rent payments. Tonight, Marcus sat on the edge of his mattress, the half-stripped sheets pooled around his ankles, and listened to the hum of his refrigerator. He had finally booked an intake appointment at a community mental health clinic, not because the memories had faded, but because he could no longer outmaneuver them. He is most afraid of the next blackout, the next rough fabric, the next cry that might pull him back into the basement, but what he is desperately hoping for is a way to sleep through the night without bracing for impact. He wants to know how to walk into a room and feel like a person who belongs there, rather than something waiting to be handled.
